sources.citation: Rasmussen, Kent. 2018. A Comparative Tone Analysis of Several Bantu D30 Languages (DR Congo). PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Arlington.
sources.note: Nothing on Bhele; cites Hartell 1993 for Bhele's seven vowels and Kutsch Lojenga 2006:456-8 for Komo/Bhele/Bila correspondences, and explicitly makes 'no claim to represent the Bantu D31 languages Bhele, Bila, and Kaiku'.

sources.citation: SIL Language & Culture Archives, search by language bhy (Wayback capture 2015-09-17).
sources.note: Listing only: one item (Bira-Huku wordlists). No Bhele phonology/orthography item archived publicly.
Nothing; names, location (Lubero territory, Nord-Kivu), dialect Bugombe, 80% lexical similarity with Kaiku.

sources.citation: Gregoire, Claire. 2003. The Bantu languages of the forest. In Nurse & Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages, p.363 (Pere D31 noun-class breakdown).
sources.note: Nothing; morphology (animacy-based number marking in Pere D31) only.

sources.citation: Kutsch Lojenga, Constance. 2003. Bila (D32). In D. Nurse & G. Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages, 450-474. London: Routledge. (Routledge companion-site text layer already on file; Bhele excerpts pp.451-453, 456-458, fn.5 saved.)
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a university library login (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Nothing on stress for Bhele (or Bila). Bhele appears only comparatively: 7-vowel member of the Amba-Bira-Bhele-Bila-Kaiku-Kango-Komo group (p.452); Komo/Bhele/Bila tone-marked cognate sets (pp.456-7, Bhele data from T. Raymond); p.458 'It seems plausible that Bila once had a two-tone system with downstep, like its genetically most closely related neighbors Komo and Bhele'; voiced obstruents show no tone-lowering effect in Komo and Bhele.

sources.citation: Hartell, Rhonda L. (ed.) 1993. Alphabets of Africa. Dakar: UNESCO-BREDA / SIL. One-page entry 'Zaire -- Bhele (Border-Bantu)' (Rosetta Project scan, archive.org rosettaproject_bhy_ortho-1).
sources.note: Nothing. Phoneme/grapheme chart (7 vowels /i e ɛ a ɔ o u/, implosives vs egressive b bh d dh, kp gb) and 'Tones: high (marked only to clarify ambiguity), low unmarked'. No mention of stress or accent.

sources.citation: Thomas, John Paul. 1992. A morphophonology of Komo: Non-tonal phenomena (UND MA thesis) / 2011 re-edition SIL Electronic Working Papers 2011-006; Thomas, J. P. 1992. Tone in Komo. Work Papers of SIL, Univ. of North Dakota Session 36: 71-160. (files on file under../komo1260/; eBhele passages excerpted)
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a university library login (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Nothing on Bhele stress (nor on Komo stress). States 'There is only a phonological description of the closely related language, eBhele in Meyer and Raymond (1981)'; scattered eBhele morphological remarks (associative la, participle lo-, initial i- in ima/ina) from T. Raymond p.c.

sources.note: Cited by Kutsch Lojenga 2003:452 and Thomas 1992 as the comparative survey covering 'Bele' (= Bhele); Raymond was the SIL linguist assigned to Bhele and supplied the tone-marked Bhele data in Kutsch Lojenga 2003; any Raymond field notes/orthography statement on Bhele would be the primary prosodic source.

sources.citation: Meyer, James & Timothy Raymond. 1981. La phonologie de la langue eBhele. Lubumbashi: Centre d'etudes linguistiques theoriques et appliquees (CELTA), Universite Nationale du Zaire (UNAZA) / Summer Institute of Linguistics.

sources.note: The only phonological description of Bhele known to Glottolog, Thomas (1992/2011) and Kutsch Lojenga (2003); an SIL phonology statement of this kind normally has a suprasegmentals section covering tone and stress. Likely held in SIL DRC (Eastern Congo Group, Bunia/Nairobi) or SIL International archives (not in the public listing) and possibly CELTA Lubumbashi.
